301.quote_or_event: “Suddenly he stopped, like the ocean at the earth as a boundary and, noble, thought to himself: ‘Shame on a brother’s murder which I, as well as he, greedy for a kingdom, more wicked even than a hunter, have undertaken.’”
301.explanation: In Hemacandra's account of the duel, Bāhubali has already beaten Bharata in every contest and has just had the cakra hurled at him. He raises his fist to crush his brother, then stops in mid-charge, condemns his own fury, and renounces the kingdom to become a monk.
301.tie_back: Valluvar says restraint only counts where anger could actually do harm. Bāhubali's fist was raised against a brother he had already defeated, so holding back meant giving up a blow that would surely have landed.
301.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book I (Ādīśvaracaritra), ch. 5, part 11, 'The fight between Bharata and Bāhubali' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)
301._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a near one-to-one illustration: the power to strike was real and fully present when Bāhubali held back.

302.quote_or_event: “He will sink through anger; he will go down through pride; delusion will block up his path; through greed he will incur dangers in both worlds.”
302.explanation: King Nami tells the disguised Indra that each of the four passions (kaṣāyas) drags down the person who harbours it, and anger comes first.
302.tie_back: This matches the Kural's first half: anger harms the one who feels it, even when it cannot touch its target. It does not match the second half, which says anger against the weak is the worst evil of all.
302.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.54 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
302._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a partial match only: Jainism condemns anger as such and does not use the Kural's distinction between anger toward the strong and toward the weak.

303.quote_or_event: “If a layman abuses a monk, he should not grow angry against him; because he would be like a child, a monk should not grow angry. If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
303.explanation: Abuse (ākrośa) is one of the twenty-two hardships (parīṣaha) a Jain monk must learn to bear. He is told neither to answer it with anger nor to store it up in his mind.
303.tie_back: 'Not take them to heart' is close to Valluvar's 'forget' (maraththal): the offence is to be dropped from the mind, not merely held back for the moment.
303.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.24–25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
303._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a strong thematic fit, although it is addressed to monks facing verbal abuse rather than to everyone, and it does not state the Kural's claim that all evils spring from anger.

304.quote_or_event: “Self is the one invincible foe, (together with the four) cardinal passions, (viz. anger, pride, deceit, and greed, they are five) and the (five) senses (make ten). These (foes), O great sage, I have regularly vanquished.”
304.explanation: Asked by Keśi who the real enemies are, Gautama names the unconquered self and the four passions, with anger listed first, as the foes to be defeated.
304.tie_back: Valluvar asks whether there is any enemy greater than anger. Gautama's answer places anger among the very few enemies that count, ranked above any outward foe.
304.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
304._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Anger is called an enemy here, which fits the Kural's question, but the passage does not mention the Kural's specific image of anger killing laughter and joy.

305.quote_or_event: “The passions are the fire; knowledge, a virtuous life, and penances are the water; sprinkled with the drops of knowledge the fire of the passions is extinguished and does not burn me.”
305.explanation: Keśi asks how Gautama puts out the frightful fire that burns embodied beings. Gautama explains that the fire is the passions (Jacobi notes that the plural 'fires' stands for the four kaṣāyas), and that he protects himself by constantly dousing them with knowledge and discipline.
305.tie_back: Valluvar tells anyone who wants to protect himself to guard against anger, or it will consume him. Gautama describes exactly that kind of guarding: he keeps the fire of passion from burning him by constantly dousing it.
305.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.50–53 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
305._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The self-protection logic is a strong fit, but the passage speaks of all four passions rather than anger alone.

306.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys humility, deceit or cheating destroys friends; but greed destroys all.”
306.explanation: The Daśavaikālika lists what each passion ruins and gives anger as the destroyer of love (prīti) between people.
306.tie_back: Valluvar's anger burns up 'the raft of kinsmen and friends'. The Jain verse names the same casualty: the bonds of affection that hold a person's circle together.
306.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.38 (English rendering as given on tattvagyan.com, 'Greed destroys all')
306._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on tattvagyan.com, a devotional Jain website rather than a scholarly edition, so the wording is that site's rendering. It matches the 'kin-raft' half of the Kural but not its fire image.

307.quote_or_event: “The ascetic jumped up angrily, thinking, ‘I’ll kill the young disciple,’ and began to run. Blind with anger, he ran against a pillar and was killed.” … “Flaming with anger like a fire with an oblation, he seized an axe with a sharp edge and ran forward … As he fell, the sharp axe fell on him and split his head in two.”
307.explanation: This is the back-story of the serpent Caṇḍakauśika. In two successive lives a man who treated his rage as a weapon was killed by it: first he ran into a pillar, then his own axe split his head. Hemacandra comments that 'anger which has a sharp continuity goes along into another birth.'
307.tie_back: Valluvar compares the man who prizes anger to someone who strikes the ground and only hurts his own hand. In Hemacandra's story the angry man wields his anger, and in the end his own axe, and the blow comes back on him.
307.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. 3, part 10, 'Episode of Caṇḍakauśika' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)
307._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a vivid narrative parallel to anger rebounding on its owner. It is a 12th-century narrative source, not canonical scripture.

308.quote_or_event: “Angry at this thought, Somaśarman, malevolent, stood the neck of a water-jar, filled with blazing coals from a funeral-pyre, on his head. Though burned severely by it, absorbed in meditation, he endured it. The fuel of karma being consumed, omniscience having arisen, he went to emancipation.”
308.explanation: The newly ordained monk Gajasukumāla, Kṛṣṇa's younger brother, is standing in meditation in a cemetery when his father-in-law places live coals on his head. He bears it without breaking his meditation and attains liberation. Afterwards Neminātha tells the grieving Kṛṣṇa, 'Do not be angry at Somaśarman.'
308.tie_back: Valluvar asks us to hold back anger even when the harm done to us is like being plunged into blazing fire. In Gajasukumāla's case the fire was literal, and he endured it without retaliating.
308.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book VIII (Nemināthacaritra), ch. 10, part 3, 'Gajasukumāla' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)
308._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a near-literal match to the Kural's fire image. Hemacandra describes Gajasukumāla's endurance in meditation rather than explicitly saying 'without anger'; the story is also told in the canonical Antakṛddaśā, which I did not check.

309.quote_or_event: “By conquering anger he obtains patience; he acquires no Karman productive of anger, and destroys the Karman he had acquired before.”
309.explanation: In the catalogue of spiritual exertions, Mahāvīra says that overcoming anger (krodhavijaya) produces patience, stops new anger-producing karma, and wears away the old.
309.tie_back: Valluvar promises that someone who never lets anger into his mind will gain whatever he desires. The Jain text also promises a reward for conquering anger, but the reward is freedom from karma rather than fulfilled wishes.
309.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.67 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
309._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The fit is reasonable but partial: Jainism treats desires themselves as bondage, so the Kural's 'attaining all one desires' does not carry over directly.

310.quote_or_event: “Bravo! you have conquered anger; bravo! you have vanquished pride; bravo! you have banished delusion; bravo! you have subdued greed. … Here (on earth) you are the highest man, Reverend sir, and hereafter you will be the highest; exempt from all blemishes you will reach Perfection.”
310.explanation: Indra drops his disguise and praises the renouncing king Nami, first of all for having conquered anger, and declares him the highest of men, bound for Perfection.
310.tie_back: Valluvar says those who have wholly given up anger are equal to renunciants. Here the renunciant is praised precisely for having conquered anger, so the conquest of anger and renunciation are presented together.
310.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.56–58 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
310._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a strong fit for the Kural's second line. The first line, that the excessively angry are as good as dead, has no direct counterpart here.
